issues.legal_issue: A statutory clause validating certain partitions does not displace a separate statutory definition of stridhana land when the two provisions address different subjects.
material_facts: A partition deed executed after the commencement of the land-ceiling law and during the period in which the law permitted such partitions was accepted as valid.
The land allotted to the wife under the deed was sought to be excluded from the husband's holding as her stridhana land.
issues.conclusion: The clause validating the partition did not override the statutory definition of stridhana land or remove the requirement that the land satisfy that definition.
issues.legal_principle: A non-obstante clause must be construed by determining its scope; where its operative subject concerns the validity of specified partitions and the other provision concerns the definition of stridhana land, the clause does not override that definition. The Court applied Aswini Kumar v. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1952 SC 369, and Madhav Rao Scindia v. Union of India, (1971) 1 SCC 85, on construing non-obstante clauses, and distinguished Sushila Devi Ammal v. State of Madras, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 462, which concerned a different provision.

predicates.partition_validated_under_special_rule: A partition was treated as valid under a special statutory rule validating specified partitions.
predicates.exclusion_depends_on_stridhana_status: A party seeks to exclude land from a holding on the ground that it qualifies as stridhana land.
predicates.validation_of_partition_does_not_displac: Validation of the partition does not displace the statutory requirements for land to qualify as stridhana land.

issues.definition: When a land-ceiling proceeding relies on a specially validated partition to claim a stridhana exclusion, the validation alone does not displace the requirements for that exclusion.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory definition of stridhana land is interpreted according to its own terms rather than by importing personal-law rights that the definition does not invoke.
material_facts: The land was allotted to a woman in a partition in recognition of her pre-existing right to maintenance under Hindu law.
The appellants relied on that maintenance right to argue that the land qualified as stridhana land under the land-ceiling law.
issues.conclusion: The woman's personal-law right to maintenance could not be used to expand the statutory definition of stridhana land.
issues.legal_principle: Definitions in land-ceiling laws apply across persons governed by different personal laws and must be given their statutory meaning unless the definition itself refers to personal law. The Court relied on M. Ramakrishnan v. State of Madras, (1979) 4 SCC 209, and Vengdasalam Pillai v. Union Territory of Pondicherry, (1985) 2 SCC 91.

predicates.land_ceiling_case: The proceeding concerns the calculation of a person's land holding under a land-ceiling law.
predicates.statutory_definition_silent_on_personal_: The statutory definition at issue does not refer to personal law.
predicates.classification_relies_on_personal_law: A party relies on a personal-law right to classify land under the statutory definition.
predicates.personal_law_cannot_expand_statutory_def: A personal-law right cannot expand the meaning of the statutory definition.

issues.definition: Where a land-ceiling definition does not invoke personal law, relying on a personal-law right does not expand that definition.

issues.legal_issue: A right to maintenance and a later allotment of land in satisfaction of that right do not establish that the woman held the land as owner or with an element of title on the relevant date.
material_facts: The woman had a right to maintenance against joint family property on the date the land-ceiling law commenced.
She had no share in the joint family property on that date and was not then in possession of the land as owner or with an element of title.
The land was allotted to her under a later partition deed in recognition of the maintenance right.
The appellants sought to treat the land as stridhana land and exclude it from the declarant's holding.
issues.conclusion: The woman was not holding the land as stridhana land on the commencement date; her maintenance right and the later allotment did not justify excluding the land from the declarant's holding.
issues.legal_principle: For the statutory definition of stridhana land, holding requires ownership or possession or enjoyment with an element of title; a maintenance claim against property is not equivalent to holding it. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Sarjoo Devi, (1977) 4 SCC 2; Bhudan Singh v. Nabi Bux, (1969) 2 SCC 481; State of Andhra Pradesh v. Mohd. Ashrafuddin, (1982) 2 SCC 1; and Hari Ram v. Babu Gokul Prasad, 1991 Supp (2) SCC 608, on the meaning of holding. It applied Rambhau v. State of Maharashtra, 1995 Supp (3) SCC 74, and the statutory provisions concerning holding, stridhana land, and notional computation of shares, including sections 3(19), 3(42), and 5(3) of the Act. It distinguished V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy, (1977) 3 SCC 99, which concerned a woman's rights under a different enactment.
